title: What Is Hidden Inside Your Phone?

fin.small: Sources: USGS, 'Ordinary Minerals Give Smartphones Extraordinary Capabilities' (2017); ITU and UNITAR, Global E-waste Monitor 2024.

parts: Your phone may hold a tiny piece of a mine in Congo.
Stay for the numbers on how little old electronics give back.
US government geologists listed the minerals behind a smartphone.
Neodymium, a rare earth, goes into the magnets for the speaker and the buzz.
Indium makes the touchscreen coating conduct. Gallium goes into some screen backlights.
But two more ingredients take you across three continents.
Lithium, often from Australia, Chile or Argentina. Tantalum, mostly from Congo, Rwanda and Brazil.
Old shoebox phones used twenty-five to thirty elements. Today's, many more.
In 2022, under a quarter of the world's electronic waste was documented as properly recycled.
And recycled e-waste covers at most one percent of rare earth demand.
Our reading: the old phone in your drawer is a tiny mine. Subscribe for the next one.
